Commentary
Embracing Model Heterogeneity for Better
Brain-Behavior Associations
Dustin Scheinost and Marisa N. Spann
Neuroimaging data can improve our understanding of the
neurobiology that underlies psychiatric disorders and putatively inform interventions (1,2). However, the associations between individual differences in brain structure and
function and individual differences in behavior and symptoms are complex. Variation in a single brain region is
unlikely to explain a person’s behavior (3). Instead,
behavior is likely embedded in the coordination between
several regions and networks. Unlike classical inferential
methods, machine learning can uncover widespread,
multivariate patterns hidden in classical methods.
Accordingly, machine learning may better capture these
associations and is increasingly being used with neuroimaging data (1,2).
Zhao et al. (4) argue that we must go further. They note that
a key limitation of many machine learning applications for
psychiatry is the handling of population heterogeneity. Within
large samples, whether patients or not, considerable heterogeneity of demographic, socioenvironmental, and physiological backgrounds shapes our brains, behaviors, and
associations. Most studies create a single model that is expected to generalize across populations. These models can
have several strengths, including handling sizable dataset
shifts (5) (i.e., “characteristic differences between the data
used to train and test a model”) and incorporating structure
and function from several networks. Nevertheless, no single
brain-behavior association or machine learning model will fit
everyone (2). Many current studies inherently ignore this population heterogeneity.
The heterogeneous machine learning framework proposed by Zhao et al. (4) uses population heterogeneity to
increase the nuance of brain-behavior models. Population
heterogeneity in neuroimaging and behavioral data are
already emerging topics for improving brain-behavior
modeling (1,2). However, the heterogeneity in brainbehavior mapping is often ignored. Heterogeneous machine learning argues that an individual’s background should
inform the appropriate models. This framework is the machine learning equivalent of adding interaction terms to a
classic statistical model. Essentially, outside variables
moderate the brain-behavior association. Heterogeneous

machine learning is data driven so that these variables can
be learned directly from the data.
This framework touches on bias and fairness in machine
learning. Bias refers to “results systematically prejudiced toward an individual or a group based on their inherent and
acquired characteristics.” In contrast, fairness is defined as
“the absence of bias” (6). However, instead of viewing a biased
model (i.e., one that only works well in a particular group) solely
as a negative, heterogeneous machine learning may view it as
part of a collection of models needed to predict behavior
across individuals. A key consideration with any biased model
is to minimize its negative impact. For example, given a
collection of biased models, adding an algorithmic layer to
determine the best model for an individual could lead to fairness. Heterogeneous machine learning advocates for considering and learning this algorithmic layer.
Heterogeneous machine learning should not be confused
with poor-performing models that do not generalize. A model
designed for a particular subgroup is different from overfitting
to a particular subgroup. An overfit model will not generalize
well to independent datasets. A model designed for a subgroup should generalize across a range of dataset shifts (e.g.,
scanner or site) except for the dimension that defined the
subgroup.
While heterogeneous machine learning is a promising
framework, some considerations exist. First, numerous factors
could show interaction terms. Discovering and testing the
most important ones is challenging. Current studies using
heterogeneous machine learning concepts simplify the problem, relying on binary or low-dimensional discrete variables.
For example, these studies have created different models for
male and female participants (2) or used data-driven approaches to cluster a sample into a few subgroups (7). Incorporating higher dimensional subgroups or continuous
variables is significantly more challenging. It is unclear how
current algorithms will handle several continuous variables as
interaction terms and whether researchers can interpret the
results.
Second, in classical inference, interactions have smaller
effect sizes than main effects. A rule of thumb suggests that 16
times the sample is needed to estimate an interaction than is
needed for the main effect (8). Brain-behavior models exhibit
modest effect sizes, and machine learning is already data
hungry. Furthermore, most available data come from Western,

educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic participants (1).
It is unclear whether we have the sample size and diversity
needed for such approaches. However, it is argued that
currently observed effect sizes are suppressed due to applying
models in a one-size-fits-all manner. Accounting for population
heterogeneity may increase observed effect sizes, thereby
increasing power.
Third, heterogeneous machine learning does not address
many of the issues that have plagued machine learning.
Common errors [like data leakage (9)] and outright fraud (10)
are possible with the framework. Similarly, models can easily

be overinterpreted and overhyped. Careful adherence to field
standards and best practices is still needed regardless of the
machine learning framework that is used.
Overall, Zhao et al. (4) provide a theorical way forward to
improve neuroimaging-based machine learning for psychiatry.
It is straightforward—in theory—and compelling. In practice,
new algorithmic development and additional training datasets
are likely needed to fully achieve the framework.
